section.heading: Scope.
section.text: This chapter applies to a pharmacy licensed in Maryland engaging in:

para.text: Compounding or mixing sterile prescription solutions or suspensions to be administered by:
Injection or infusion;
Irrigations for internal body cavities;
Ophthalmic;
Pulmonary inhalation;
Baths and soaks for live organs and tissues; or
Implant routes;

Compounding of Hazardous Drugs when U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding––Sterile Preparations states that U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings would apply; and

Compounding of radiopharmaceuticals, when U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding––Sterile Preparations states that USP Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging would apply.

section.heading: Incorporation by Reference.
section.text: In this chapter, the following documents are incorporated by reference:

para.text: U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding—Sterile Preparations (USP 797 Standards), which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended);
U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings (USP 800 Standards), which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended); and
U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals—Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging, which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended).
In this chapter, the following terms have the meanings indicated.
Terms Defined.
Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient.

“Active pharmaceutical ingredient” means any substance or mixture of substances intended to be used in the compounding of a preparation, thereby becoming the active ingredient in that preparation, and furnishing pharmacological activity or other direct effect in:
The diagnosis;
The cure;
The mitigation;
The treatment;
The prevention of disease in humans and animals; or
How the structure and function of the body is affected.
“Active pharmaceutical ingredient” does not include a conventionally manufactured drug product that is typically manufactured from an active pharmaceutical ingredient.
“Adverse event” means:
Any adverse patient outcome related to the sterile compounding process; or
Evidence of environmental contamination, including microbial contamination above the threshold set forth in USP 797 Standards.

“Anteroom” means an International Standards Organization Class 8 or cleaner room with fixed walls and doors where personnel hand hygiene, garbing procedures, and other activities that generate high particulate levels may be performed. The anteroom is the transition room between the unclassified area of the facility and the buffer room.
Batch.

“Batch” means a preparation compounded in advance of receipt of a prescription, or a preparation compounded in a supply that will be used on more than one dispensing to a patient or patients or any preparation compounded in excess of the filling of an individual prescription.
“Batch” includes a limited quantity of identical preparations compounded in a single, discrete process, by the same individuals, carried out during one limited time period.
“Beyond-use date” means the date, or hour and the date, after which a CSP must not be used, stored, or transported. The date is determined from the date and time the preparation is compounded.
“Biological safety cabinet” means a ventilated containment unit:
Suitable for work involving agents that pose higher risk of exposure to operators during compounding; and
Used when there is a need for protection of the preparation, personnel, and environment.

“Buffer room” means an International Standards Organization Class 7 or cleaner room with fixed walls and doors where primary engineering controls that generate and maintain an International Standards Organization Class 5 environment are physically located. The buffer room may only be accessed through the anteroom or another buffer room.
“Classified area” means an area that maintains an air quality classification based on the ISO standards required by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.
“Cleanroom suite” means a classified area that consists of both an anteroom and a buffer room.

“Closed-system drug-transfer device” means a drug-transfer device that mechanically prohibits the transfer of environmental contaminants into the system and the escape of hazardous drugs or vapor concentrations outside of the system.

“Compounded sterile preparation (CSP)” means a medication preparation intended to be sterile that is created by combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance.

“Compounding” means the process of combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance to create a sterile preparation:
As the result of a practitioner’s prescription drug order or initiative based on the practitioner/patient relationship in the course of professional practice;
For the purpose of, or incidental to, research, teaching, or chemical analysis and not for the sale or dispensing of the drug or device; or
In anticipation of a prescription drug order based on routine, regularly observed prescribing patterns.

“Compounding aseptic isolator” means a type of restricted access barrier that uses high efficiency particulate air filtration to provide an ISO Class 5 unidirectional air environment designed for compounding of sterile non-hazardous drugs.

“Compounding aseptic containment isolator” means a type of restricted-access barrier that uses high efficiency particulate air filtration to provide an ISO Class 5 unidirectional air environment designed for the compounding of sterile hazardous drugs.
“Designee” means a public agency or private entity recognized by the Board to conduct sterile compounding inspections that is trained in:
USP 797 Standards;
FDA good manufacturing practices approved by the Board to conduct inspections of nonresident pharmacies that perform sterile compounding; or
Both §B(15)(a) and (b) of this regulation.
“Dynamic operating conditions” means conditions in the compounding area in which operating personnel are present and simulating or performing compounding activities.

“Expiration” means the time period during which a manufactured product is expected to remain stable, or retain its identity, strength, quality, and purity, when it is properly stored according to its labeled storage conditions.

“Hazardous drug” means a drug included on the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health list of antineoplastic and other hazardous drugs in healthcare settings, which are identified by at least one of the following six criteria:
Carcinogenicity;
Teratogenicity or developmental toxicity;
Reproductive toxicity in humans;
Organ toxicity at low dose in humans or animals;
Genotoxicity; or
New drugs that mimic existing hazardous drugs in structure or toxicity.
“Healthcare practitioner intermediary” means an entity or person that connects healthcare providers with patients, payers, or other relevant parties.

“High efficiency particulate air filtration” means a filtration system that has the ability to capture particles at its most penetrating particle size and removing 99.97 percent of particles at .03 micrometers.
“International Organization for Standardization class” means an air-quality classification from the International Organization for Standardization.

“Laminar airflow system” means a device or zone within a buffer room that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 or better air quality environment for sterile compounding. The system provides a unidirectional high efficiency particulate air-filtered airflow.

“Laminar airflow workbench” means a device that is a type of laminar airflow system that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 or better air quality environment for sterile compounding. The device provides a unidirectional high efficiency particulate air-filtered airflow.

“Media-fill test” means a simulation used to qualify processes and personnel engaged in sterile compounding to ensure that the processes and personnel are able to prepare compounding sterile preparations without contamination.

“National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health list” means the list maintained by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health of antineoplastic and other hazardous drugs used in healthcare.
“Parenteral” means routes of drug administration or fluid administration other than via the gastrointestinal tract.
“Pharmacist” means an individual who is licensed to practice pharmacy regardless of the location where the activities of practice are performed.
“Pharmacy” means an establishment in which prescription or nonprescription drugs or devices are compounded, dispensed, or distributed.
“Primary engineering control” means a device or zone that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 air quality environment for sterile compounding.
“Pyrogen testing” means an analysis of sterile preparations for the presence of cell material from microbiological organisms in sufficient quantity to elicit a febrile reaction.

“Restricted-access barrier system” means an enclosure that provides high efficiency particulate air-filtered International Standards Organization Class 5 unidirectional air that allows for the ingress or egress, or both, of materials through defined openings that have been designed and validated to preclude the transfer of contamination, and that generally are not to be opened during operations.
“Secondary engineering control” means a space which provides a classified area where primary engineering controls are placed.
“Sterile” means free from viable microorganisms.

“Sterile compounding” means the process of combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance to create a preparation using aseptic techniques in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.
“Total parenteral nutrition” means providing nutritional needs by the parenteral route for a patient who is unable to ingest sufficient calories.
“USP 797 Standards” means standards set forth in the U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding — Sterile Preparations.
“US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards” means the standards set forth in US Pharmacopeia General Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings.
“US Pharmacopeia 825 Standards” means the standards set forth in US Pharmacopeia General Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging.

section.heading: Pharmacy Environment.
section.text: The compounding, preparation, and dispensing of compounded sterile preparations shall be accomplished in a pharmacy environment subject to State and federal laws, regulations, and standards.

section.heading: General Requirements.
section.text: A licensed supervising pharmacist who has appropriate practical and didactic training in compounding sterile preparations, cleanroom technology, laminar flow technology, quality assurance techniques, and clinical application of intravenous drug therapy shall control and supervise the section of the pharmacy that prepares compounded sterile preparations and is responsible for, at a minimum, the following:

para.text: Preparation of compounded sterile preparations within the pharmacy or decentralized pharmacy;

Storage of materials pertinent to the preparation of compounded sterile preparations, including drugs, chemicals, and biologicals, and the establishment of specifications for procurement of the materials;
Labeling of containers of compounded sterile preparations compounded within or dispensed by the pharmacy;

Recording of transactions of the pharmacy as may be applicable to State and federal laws and regulations, as may be necessary to maintain accurate control over, and accountability for, pharmaceutical materials;
Overseeing an initial and ongoing training and competency program for all staff with duties within the cleanroom in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .14 of this chapter;
Ensuring engineering controls and equipment utilized for compounding meet the US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .09 of this chapter;
Ensuring policies and procedures, provided in US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .12 of this chapter, are implemented, maintained, and reviewed on an annual basis; and
Overseeing a quality assurance and quality control program to monitor:
Adherence to policies and procedures;
Prevention and detection of errors and quality issues;
Investigation of complaints and reported adverse events; and
Corrective actions and recall programs.

section.heading: Special Handling, Packaging, Labeling, and Beyond Use Dating.

para.text: The pharmacy shall make available special handling and packaging materials to maintain container integrity and drug stability of the prepared prescription orders, including hazardous sterile preparations, during handling and administration to the patient including:
A reasonable effort to provide tamper-evident packaging on compounded sterile preparations;
Proper in-transit storage consistent with preparation labeling;

For medications not distributed to a Healthcare Practitioner Intermediary, the enclosure of information to inform the patient if the prescription is a temperature sensitive medication that is at risk for damage due to extreme hot or cold temperatures or moisture; and
Delivery to the patient within a reasonable time.
The dispensed container for any compounded sterile preparation shall include labeling according to State law and regulations, in addition to the following information:
The date of the preparation unless otherwise readily retrievable from prescription records;
Time prepared, if applicable;
The pertinent requirements for proper storage;
The name of the prescriber, unless in an inpatient hospital setting;
The name of the patient;
Directions for use;
The name of the base solution for infusion preparations;
The name and concentration or amount of active drugs contained in the final sterile preparation;

The name or identifying initials of the individual who prepared the compounded sterile preparation and the pharmacist who checked the compounded sterile preparation unless otherwise readily retrievable from prescription records;
The name, address, and telephone number of the pharmacy unless in an inpatient hospital facility;
The beyond-use date and time of the compounded sterile preparation, and if no time is stated, the time is presumed to be at 11:59 p.m. of the stated date;
Any ancillary and cautionary instructions as needed; and
A pertinent warning consistent with applicable federal and State law of the presence of hazardous drugs including instructions for safe handling and proper disposal.

A pharmacy compounding sterile preparations shall provide a 24-hour telephone number to allow its patients or other health care providers who may be administering its prescriptions to contact its pharmacists.
Beyond-use Dates.
A pharmacy shall use timeframes for beyond-use dates as determined by US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 1 or 2 Standards; and

Beyond-use dates greater than those set forth in US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 1 or 2 Standards shall comply with US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 3 Standards and appropriate reference materials cited in Regulation .16 of this chapter.
Patient Prescription Records.
The pharmacy shall maintain records of patient prescriptions.
Patient prescription records shall contain:
Available medical information consistent with prevailing pharmacy standards; and
The complete record of the formulations of the solutions that were compounded.
The pharmacy shall keep completed patient prescription records in a retrievable manner for at least 5 years, either:
At the inspection site; or
So as to be immediately retrievable by computer or other electronic means.
Compounded Sterile Preparations Records.
For a pharmacy preparing compounded sterile preparations, the following records shall be maintained for at least 5 years:
The training and competency evaluation of:
Pharmacy employees in sterile preparation procedures; and
Non-pharmacy employees responsible for the maintenance and cleaning of the cleanroom;
Refrigerator and freezer temperatures;
Incubator temperatures when in use;
Certification of the classified area, including ISO 5 workstations cleanrooms, and other controlled rooms, such as hazardous drug storage areas;
Other daily facility quality control logs specific to the pharmacy's policies and procedures, such as:
Cleaning logs for facilities and equipment;
Cleanroom pressures; and
Temperature and humidity;
Records documenting inspection for expired or recalled pharmaceutical preparations, components, or raw ingredients;
Trending of microbiological growth and actions taken for adverse trending;
Investigations, corrective actions, and preventative measures for any adverse event;
Certificates of analysis of active pharmaceutical ingredient components of compounded sterile preparations, and microbial growth;
Safety data sheets of active pharmaceutical ingredients utilized in the process of sterile compounding and other chemicals and cleaning agents utilized in the cleanroom suite;
Documentation of recalls initiated by the pharmacy of compounded sterile products;
Compounding and preparation records, including:
Worksheets;
Processing checklists;
Procedure sign-off forms; and
Final check logs;

Master formulation record as described by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for all compounded sterile preparations prepared from nonsterile ingredients or compounded sterile preparations prepared for more than one patient; and
The results and documentation of applicable end product sterilization, testing, and validation.

In addition to the records requirement in §B(1) of this regulation, for batch compounded sterile preparations, a pharmacy compounding sterile batch preparations for future use shall have records indicating the:
Drug and ingredient names;
Lot numbers;
Expiration dates of components;
Drug/diluent amounts;
Assigned beyond-use dates; and
Date on which the compounded sterile batch preparations were prepared.
A pharmacy may prepare batched sterile preparations for future use before receiving a valid written prescription or medication order.
Batch preparation of specific compounded sterile preparations is acceptable if the pharmacy:

Compounds limited quantities based on a documented history of valid prescriptions or physician orders that have been generated solely within an established professional prescriber-patient-pharmacist relationship; and
Maintains the prescription on file for each compounded sterile preparation dispensed.
Batch preparation labeling shall meet the requirements of Regulation .06 of this chapter.
Record keeping of batch preparations shall meet the requirements of Regulation .07 of this chapter.
Classified Area.
The pharmacy shall have a classified area that meets USP 797, 800, or 825 Standards, as applicable.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the classified area is:
Accessible only to designated personnel; and
Used only for the preparation of compounded sterile preparations, or other tasks that require a classified area.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the classified area is:
Structurally isolated from other areas within the pharmacy by means of restricted entry or access; and
Air conditioned to maintain the temperature and humidity of the classified area according to USP 797 Standards.
If compounding occurs outside of a cleanroom, the area and procedures shall meet US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for a segregated compounding area or for immediate use administration.
Buffer Room. The pharmacy shall ensure that the buffer room in the classified area:
Meets USP 797 Standards for design and USP 797 Standards for performance criteria quality for buffer rooms;
Contains no sinks or floor drains;
Contains work surfaces constructed of smooth, impervious materials, such as stainless steel or molded plastic, so that the work surfaces may be readily cleaned and sanitized;
If hazardous drugs are used in compounded preparations, contains room or rooms equipped with special pressurization requirements consistent with USP 797 and 800 Standards;
Has in place appropriate environmental engineering control devices capable of maintaining USP 797 Standards for air-quality during routine operations and under dynamic operating conditions; and
Contains the following equipment:
Primary engineering controls validated to maintain International Standards Organization (ISO) Class 5 compounding environment during routine operations and under dynamic operating conditions;
Waste containers that are approved by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for used needles and syringes, and for hazardous drug waste; and
Ancillary supplies required for proper compounding.
Anteroom. The pharmacy shall ensure that the anteroom in the classified area:
Meets USP 797 Standards for design and USP 797 performance criteria quality standards for anterooms; and
Contains the following equipment:
A sink with hot and cold running water:
At least a meter away from a primary engineering control within a segregated compounding area; or
If outside the cleanroom suite, the pharmacy shall have a policy and procedure on how to maintain hand hygiene while entering the cleanroom and donning protective garb;
Waste containers; and
An eyewash station or sink design suitable for flushing an eye injury.
The pharmacy shall provide at least the following equipment that is maintained in working order:
Adequate refrigerator and freezer space (if applicable);
A sink for hand hygiene and if applicable, cleaning equipment;
Appropriate waste containers for:
Used needles and syringes; and
Hazardous drug waste including disposable personal protective equipment used in its preparation, if applicable;
Primary engineering controls that meet USP 797 Standards, dedicated for products other than hazardous drugs;

If applicable to types of preparations compounded, biological safety cabinet, or compounding aseptic containment isolator that meets USP 797 Standards, dedicated for use with hazardous or radiopharmaceutical sterile preparations;
Appropriate filters and filtration equipment; and
A dedicated space or equipment for light/dark field examination.
All equipment, devices, and monitoring tools utilized in the sterile compounding process shall be:
Maintained in working order;
Calibrated; and
Certified, where appropriate.

section.heading: Minimum Requirements for Supplies.
section.text: A pharmacy engaging in compounding sterile preparations shall maintain adequate stock levels of the following supplies according to USP 797 Standards, including but not limited to:

para.text: Garb for sterile compounding including:
Sterile gloves;
Masks;
Non-shedding gowns;
Shoe covers;
Hair covers;
Beard covers; and
Other garb and personal protective equipment for handling hazardous drugs as required per US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
Disposable syringes and needles in necessary sizes;
Cleaning agents as specified in USP 797 Standards including:
Disinfectant and sporicidal cleaning agents; and
Water, if utilized as part of the primary engineering control cleaning process, such as for rinsing surfaces or diluting cleaning agents, which shall be sterile;
Disposable lint free towels;
Hand washing materials, including:
Nail picks;
Antimicrobial skin cleanser; and
Alcohol-based hand rub;
Sesventyt at percent sterile isopropyl or ethyl alcohol;
Supplies necessary for the aseptic preparation of compounded sterile preparations;
A hazardous waste spill kit, if applicable; and
Closed system vial transfer devices (CSTD), as required for hazardous compounding, if applicable.

section.heading: Minimum Requirements for Policies and Procedures.

para.text: The pharmacy shall ensure that a supervising pharmacist shall maintain a policy and procedure manual, reviewed annually, that sets forth in detail the pharmacy’s standard operating procedures with regard to compounding sterile preparations.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the policy and procedure manual that sets forth the standard operating procedures with regard to compounding sterile preparations is implemented and adhered to.
The policy and procedure manual shall include policies and procedures governing the following:
A risk-management program which includes documentation of outcomes including, but not limited to:
Environmental excursions;
Adverse drug reactions;
Preparation contamination; and
Recalls of compounded sterile preparations prepared by the pharmacy.
Security measures ensuring that the premises where sterile compounded preparations are stored and prepared are secured, to prevent access by unauthorized personnel;
Equipment including, but not limited to:
Procedures for use;
Documentation of appropriate certifications; and
Documentation of appropriate calibration and preventive maintenance if applicable;
Sanitation and cleaning standards and procedures;
Maintenance and availability of reference materials as set forth in Regulation .16 of this chapter;
Information concerning drug:
Preparation;
Storage and handling;
Dispensing;
Labeling;
Beyond-use dating;
Release testing and verification;
Delivery;
Destruction;
Recalls; and
Returns;
Patient record keeping as set forth in Regulation .07 of this chapter;
Facility and equipment control monitoring as set forth in Regulation .07 of this chapter;
Facility certification and viable testing program, as described by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Handling, dispensing, and documentation of investigational drugs;
A quality assurance program;
Training verification procedures, including:
Gloved thumb and fingertip sampling;
Visual observation for adherence to aseptic technique; and
Media-fill testing with post gloved fingertip and thumb, and surface sampling;
Description of appropriate garb donning and doffing processes;
Conduct guidelines for personnel in the controlled areas;
Personnel responsibilities including:
Pharmacists who are not physically involved in the compounding process;
Compounding staff; and
Cleaning and maintenance staff who have access to the cleanroom;
Patient education, unless in an inpatient setting;
Protocols and procedures to maintain the integrity of the cleanroom suite and the primary engineering controls;
Handling of hazardous drugs as per US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards, if applicable, including:
Utilizing the proper equipment and supplies;
A statement that compounding shall be conducted within a properly certified biological safety cabinet or compounding aseptic containment isolator;
Proper use of personal protective equipment; and
Proper techniques to prevent both contamination of the preparation and chemical exposure of the individual preparing the medication;
Segregation of biological and hazardous material from other compounding activities to prevent cross-contamination, if applicable;
The disposal of infectious materials or materials containing hazardous drugs or waste, as per USP 800 Standards, if applicable;
Written documentation of policy and procedure changes based on data gathered from quality assurance evaluations; and
Assurance of the sterility and stability of compounded sterile preparations including end-product testing and sterilization, if applicable.

section.heading: Cleanroom Garbing.
section.text: When compounding sterile preparations, individuals shall comply with the following standards:

para.text: Sequencing of garbing that complies with USP 797 and 800 Standards, as applicable;
Thorough handwashing before gowning;
Wearing clean room garb inside the designated area at all times, which consists of:
A non-shedding coverall or gown;
Head and facial hair covers;
A face mask;
Shoe covers; and
Other personal protective equipment required for the handling and preparation of hazardous drugs, in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
Cleanroom garb, with the exception of sterile gloves, shall be donned and removed outside the designated cleanroom area;
Personal protective equipment and garb required for the handling and preparation of hazardous drugs shall be removed, in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
All jewelry that can be physically removed, shall be removed;
Sterile powder-free gloves are required;
Make-up, cosmetic lotions, creams, ointments, false nails, and other cosmetic accessories may not be worn in the cleanroom; and
Nails shall be natural and short, not extending past the nail bed.

section.heading: Training of Staff, Patient, and Caregiver.

para.text: The pharmacy shall make counseling available to the patient or primary caregiver, or both, concerning:
Proper use of compounded sterile preparations and related supplies dispensed by the pharmacy;
Signs of contamination or other issues seen in CSPs; and
Proper disposal of:
Excess medications;
Biohazards;
Sharps; and
Hazardous drug waste.

The pharmacy shall ensure that pharmacy personnel engaging in compounding sterile preparations are trained and demonstrate competence in the safe handling and compounding of sterile preparations, including hazardous drugs, if applicable.
The pharmacy shall maintain records of training and demonstrated competence for individual employees for 5 years.
The pharmacy shall ensure the continuing competence of pharmacy personnel engaged in compounding sterile preparations.
A pharmacy that compounds sterile preparations shall comply with the following training requirements:

The pharmacy shall establish and follow a written program of annual training and performance evaluation designed to ensure that individuals working in the designated area have the knowledge and skills necessary to perform the assigned tasks properly and include at least the following:
Aseptic technique with gloved fingertip and thumb sampling, and media-fill testing with post gloved thumb and fingertip and surface sampling at a minimum frequency defined by USP 797 Standards;
Pharmaceutical calculations and terminology;
Sterile compounding documentation process;
Quality assurance procedures;
Aseptic preparation procedures, including principles of unidirectional airflow;
Proper hand cleansing, gowning, and gloving techniques;
General conduct within the controlled area;
Cleaning, sanitizing, and maintaining:
Equipment used in the classified area; and
The cleanroom suite;
Sterilization techniques, if applicable;
Container and closure system selection; and
Identifying and reporting problems, failures, and errors to designated individuals.
Individuals assigned to the classified area shall successfully complete practical skills training in aseptic technique and aseptic area practices prior to compounding medication for patients.
Evaluations shall include:
Written testing;
Observation for adherence to aseptic technique and aseptic area policies and procedures; and
Media-fill testing with gloved fingertip and thumb sampling, and surface sampling as set forth in §E(1)(a) of this regulation.

A pharmacy with only one pharmacist performing compounding shall establish and maintain training and competencies through a third party who is competent in the requirements set forth in this chapter and US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.

Ensuring that all individuals who enter the cleanroom for cleaning, maintenance, or any other reason shall, at a minimum, have demonstrated competence and understanding of appropriate garbing, hand hygiene, conduct, and duties within the cleanroom.
Ensuring that all individuals responsible for handling, storing, packing, and transporting of CSPs shall be trained in duties associated with their position.
The completion, upon initial hire, evaluations as set forth in §E(1) of this regulation, including three passing consecutive gloved fingertip and thumb samplings.

section.heading: Quality Assurance.
section.text: The pharmacy shall ensure that the CSP retains its potency and sterility throughout the assigned beyond-use date through a written quality assurance program that includes:

para.text: A reasonable effort by the pharmacist to assure that compounded sterile preparations shall be kept under appropriate controlled conditions before dispensing, during transport, and at the location of use by providing adequate labeling and verbal or written instructions regarding proper storage and administration, as set forth by the product manufacturer and established standards and literature, with each compounded sterile preparation dispensed;
The sterile compounding process, distribution, storage, administration, and directions for use for each type of preparation dispensed;
Primary engineering controls certification by a trained and qualified operator, according to US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Secondary engineering control certification by a trained and qualified operator according to US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Environmental sampling for microbial organisms is performed according to methods and schedules specified by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Trending of microbial growth observed during viable testing;

A formal written process for reviewing and investigating environmental excursions occurring, both with personnel and within the cleanroom, including suspected sources of contamination, corrective and preventative actions, follow-up actions, associated recalls, and reporting to State and federal agencies, as required by law or regulation;

The proper disposal in accordance with accepted professional standards and applicable State and federal laws of unused drugs and materials used in the preparation of compounded sterile preparations, including:
Hazardous drugs;
Radiopharmaceutical waste; and
Any potentially contaminated materials;
A written review process to document, report, and evaluate compliance with this chapter; and

J A process that complies with applicable US Pharmacopeia Standards for performing sterility, potency, pyrogen and endotoxin testing, or other quality attributes, for applicable compounded sterile preparations.

section.heading: Reference Library.
section.text: Minimum reference materials in a pharmacy shall include:

para.text: United States Pharmacopeia, General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding—Sterile Preparations;
United States Pharmacopeia, General Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings;
United States Pharmacopeia, General Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging;
Other applicable reference materials in order to perform sterile compounding;
Reference materials containing drug stability and compatibility data;
Reference materials concerning drug interactions and incompatibility; and
Reference materials containing drug dosing for veterinary patients, if applicable.
The Board shall inspect pharmacies located in Maryland at least annually.
The pharmacy shall provide as part of the inspection process:
Documents, reports, and information required in accordance with this chapter; and
Any other information requested to ensure compliance with USP 797 Standards.
Non-resident Pharmacies. Within 90 days before the date of application, inspections may be conducted by:
A designee of the Board;
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration; or
Another appropriate state entity which indicates compliance with USP 797 Standards.
The Board or designee shall inspect nonresident pharmacies upon initial application and upon renewal.
The Board may inspect a pharmacy at any time to:
Verify compliance with permit requirements; or
Investigate a complaint.

The Board may reference guidance documents issued by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) when inspecting and reviewing compounding practices not specifically outlined in this chapter or a chapter of US Pharmacopeia.
Document and perform routine testing as required by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for the appropriate categories of sterile compounded preparations; and
Report to the Board within 5 calendar days:
Adverse events that have been discovered including corrective actions taken or proposed;
Deficiencies related to the sterile compounding process;
Disciplinary actions in other states or by other state agencies;
Changes in accreditation status;
Disciplinary actions taken against a pharmacist or technician who is an owner, operator, or employee of the pharmacy; and
Disciplinary actions taken against any other permit, or any other authorization, held by the pharmacy permit holder.

section.heading: Office Use.
section.text: Unless otherwise authorized, a person that prepares and distributes sterile compounded medications for office use into, out of, or within the State shall hold:

para.text: A manufacturer’s permit or other registration as designated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to ensure the safety of sterile compounded medications for office use; and
If applicable, a wholesale distributor’s permit, issued by the Board under Health Occupations Article, Title 12, Subtitle 6C, Annotated Code of Maryland.
